Else
ĕls
adv. and conj. (otherwise; besides; in Scripture chiefly in the divine formula there is none else)
From Anglo-Saxon elles, otherwise — a genitive form of a lost adjective meaning other, cognate with Latin alius. The same root gives alien and alias.

Biblical Definition

Else reaches its height in Isaiah, where it becomes the vocabulary of monotheism. God says it of Himself, again and again, and each time it excludes not merely rival worship but rival existence: “I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me” (Isa 45:5). That last clause is addressed to Cyrus, a pagan king who did not know the God who was arming him — so the sovereignty asserted extends over rulers who have never heard of it. The same chapter turns the exclusion into an invitation: “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else” (Isa 45:22) — the verse under which Charles Spurgeon was converted in a Colchester snowstorm. In other places else marks the fork in a road: “either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). There is no third option in view. The word's whole work is to close off alternatives.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines else as otherwise, in the other case, or besides — noting that it excludes all but the thing named.

expand to see more

ELSE, a. or pron. Other; one or something beside; as, who else is coming?

ELSE, adv. Otherwise; in the other case; if the fact were different.

Repent, or else I will come unto thee quickly. Rev. ii.

2. Beside; except that mentioned; as, nowhere else.

Note. From the Saxon elles, otherwise, of the same root with the Latin alius.

Key Scripture

Isa 45:5 — "I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:"

Isa 45:22 — "Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else."

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Luk 16:13 — "No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Modern Corruption

The exclusivity of Isaiah's none else is treated as ancient Israelite polemic rather than a truth claim, and religious pluralism supplies a tolerance Scripture nowhere offers.

expand to see more

The pluralist reading holds that Isaiah 45 records one nation's devotional preference for its own deity, and that a mature faith today will hear it as poetry rather than as a claim about what exists. The chapter forecloses that. The God speaking claims to have raised up a Persian king by name before he was born, to form light and create darkness, and to be the only Saviour there is — and He addresses these claims to the ends of the earth, not to Israel alone. A statement designed from the outset to include every nation cannot be reduced to one nation's house style.

Mat 6:24 applies the same exclusivity to the heart. The Lord does not warn against loving money too much; He says no man can serve two masters, and that the attempt always resolves into hating one. Modern discipleship talk that speaks of balancing priorities has quietly denied the sentence. And Isa 45:22 shows why the exclusivity is good news rather than bad: because there is none else, the invitation can be issued to the ends of the earth without qualification. A God who were one option among several could save only some; a God beside whom there is none else can say look unto me, and be ye saved, and mean everyone who looks.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-Saxon elles, otherwise, cognate with Latin alius; rendering Hebrew od (H5750), yet, still, in the formula en od, there is no more, and Greek ei de me, but if not.

expand to see more

Anglo-Saxon elles — otherwise; from the same Indo-European root as Latin alius, other, whence alien and alias.

Hebrew en od — literally “there is not yet”, that is, there is no other; the refrain of Isa 45:5, 6, 14, 18, 21, 22.

Hebrew zulah (H2108) — besides, except; “there is no God beside me” (Isa 45:5).

Greek ei de me — “but if not”, rendered or else; the alternative branch in Mat 6:24 and Luk 16:13.

Greek allos (G243) — other, another of the same kind; the Greek cousin of Latin alius and of English else.

Usage

"“I am the LORD, and there is none else” — a claim about what exists, not a preference."

"“Look unto me, and be ye saved… there is none else” — exclusivity is what makes the offer universal."

"“Or else he will hold to the one” — no third road between God and mammon."
